title: Correct, or be kind
hookLine: if you can, correct them; if not, kindness was given you for this (Meditations 9.11)

cards: A friend says something you're fairly sure is wrong. Not dangerous, just wrong: a bad plan, a mistaken idea about a coworker, a choice about their kids. You can feel the correction loading in your mouth.
And then a second voice: is this the moment? Will they hear it? Marcus met that fork too.
In book nine he wrote down what to do when correcting doesn't work.

teach.h: IF YOU CAN, CORRECT BY TEACHING.
teach.b: If you can, Marcus writes, set them right by teaching. Correction isn't forbidden; a friend who never tells you the truth isn't much of a friend.

teach.h: IF NOT, KINDNESS WAS GIVEN FOR THIS.
teach.b: But if you can't, remember that kindness was given to you for exactly this. Not as decoration, not as a personality trait, but as equipment for the moment correction fails. Then the surprising part.

teach.h: EVEN THE GODS ARE KIND TO THEM.
teach.b: Even the gods, Marcus says, are kind to such people. They help them to health, to wealth, to reputation; that's how generous they are. Whatever you believe about the gods, look at the logic.
If the highest powers keep helping people who get things wrong, then kindness can't be a prize for being right. It's given to the wrong as well. And the last line: it's in your power too, he says.
Or tell me: who's stopping you?
His point: no circumstance can take away the ability to be kind. The other person can refuse your correction. Your kindness is yours to give, whether they take it well or not.
It's a close cousin of the third door, from book eight. Here the second door gets a warmer name. Not bear: be kind.

how: People who draw on this entry often decide deliberately whether a correction can actually be heard; when it can't, they choose a concrete kindness instead of repeating the point.

o: punish a mistake so it won't happen again
set someone right by teaching, if they can hear it
prove you were right and win the argument

games.q: correct, or be kind — tap the pairs.
p: kind even to those who err
no one can block your kindness

s: the first branch is: if you can, correct them by teaching.
he says even the gods are kind to people who get things wrong
they help them to health, wealth and reputation, he writes.

games.q: your brother is set on a plan you think is a mistake. you've said so plainly, and he isn't listening. you're Marcus. what now?
o: remember kindness was given you for this, and be kind.
games.why: if you can't correct them, Marcus writes, remember that kindness was given you for exactly this; even the gods are kind to such people.

practice: Think of one person you've wanted to correct lately, and ask honestly: could they hear it, and is it yours to give?

If yes, picture saying it once, plainly and warmly, then letting it go; if no, set the point down without keeping score and choose one small, concrete kindness for them instead. Hold your choice for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: Correct. Marcus's two branches: if you can, correct by teaching; if you can't, remember that kindness was given you for this. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: kindness, goodwill. Marcus says it was given to us for this.

carryVoice: Your line: who's stopping you. A correction can be refused; kindness is still yours to give. See you tomorrow.
